title: Episode 7: Merge Conflicts Are Not Scary
description: Why conflicts happen, how to read conflict markers, and resolving them confidently.
concepts: What a merge conflict is: two changes to the same lines
Why conflicts are normal and not a sign of failure
The analogy: two people editing the same paragraph of a shared document
Reading conflict markers: "your version" versus "their version"
Resolving a conflict in the GitHub web editor
Resolving a conflict using git on the command line
The git merge, git status, git add, git commit workflow for conflicts
How to prevent conflicts: communication, small PRs, frequent pulls
What happens if you get stuck: asking for help is always OK
Using gh pr checks and gh pr diff to inspect conflicts from the terminal
Confidence building: your first conflict resolution is the hardest
transcriptText:
[ALEX]
Welcome back. Today we're talking about merge conflicts, and I want to start by lowering the temperature right away. Merge conflicts are normal. They are not proof that you broke Git, and they are not a sign that you are bad at collaboration.

[JAMIE]
That helps, because the phrase merge conflict sounds dramatic.

[ALEX]
It does. But in practice, a merge conflict just means Git found two overlapping changes and needs a human decision. This lesson is about understanding what that means, how to prevent conflicts when you can, and how to resolve them calmly when they show up.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
A quick orientation before we dig in. This chapter pairs well with a short companion episode called Merge Conflicts Are Not Scary, and there are also related appendices on advanced Git and a VS Code reference. The authoritative references behind this lesson are GitHub Docs on resolving merge conflicts and the Git book's section on basic merge conflicts.

[JAMIE]
So this is one of those topics where the course teaches the workflow, but learners can also cross-check with official documentation.

[ALEX]
Exactly. And that matters, especially if you're contributing in open source or working across GitHub, Git, and VS Code.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
The core idea is simple. A merge conflict happens when two people changed the same part of the same file in different ways, and Git cannot safely choose which version should win.

[JAMIE]
So Git can merge some things automatically, just not all things.

[ALEX]
Right. If I edit line 5 and you edit line 80, Git can usually combine those changes without trouble. But if we both change the same sentence, the same table row, the same function body, or one person deletes something while another person edits it, Git stops and asks for help.

[JAMIE]
Can you give a tiny example?

[ALEX]
Sure. Suppose one person changes a button label to say Submit form, and another changes that exact same line to say Send message. Git sees two different truths for one location. That is the conflict.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
This chapter uses a controlled practice exercise, which is a smart teaching choice. Instead of waiting for a stressful real-world conflict, learners get one small challenge designed just for practice.

[JAMIE]
What does that challenge look like?

[ALEX]
There is one challenge in this chapter, designed to take under ten minutes. The evidence for completion is an issue-linked pull request and a completion comment. The learning pattern is observe, resolve, verify.

[JAMIE]
That's nice and concrete.

[ALEX]
Very. The challenge is to resolve conflict markers in a practice file, then open the linked pull request. Learners are told to use a short-lived branch named in the same style as the previous chapter, something like fix slash your-name dash issue-number.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's walk through that challenge slowly, because I think that's where many learners need the most reassurance.

[ALEX]
Absolutely. The goal is to identify the three conflict markers in a practice file, decide which content to keep, remove the markers, and submit a clean pull request.

There is also an important learning point here about AI. Sometimes an AI tool confidently generates code or text that conflicts with human-written work. Resolving merge conflicts is not only a human teamwork skill. It is also part of supervising and correcting AI-generated changes safely.

[JAMIE]
That's a great framing. Conflict resolution is really decision-making.

[ALEX]
Exactly. In the exercise, learners work either in their Learning Room repository on GitHub.com using the web editor, or in VS Code if they cloned the repository locally.

Before starting, they open their assigned challenge issue. The issue tells them which practice file contains the conflict markers.

Then the steps are very specific.

First, open the practice file named in the issue.

Second, search the file for less-than signs repeated seven times, the marker that begins with left angle brackets. That start marker shows where the conflict begins.

Third, read the text between the opening marker and the line of equals signs. That block is your version, meaning the current branch version.

Fourth, read the text between the equals signs and the closing marker made of greater-than signs. That block is their version, meaning the incoming branch version.

Fifth, decide what to keep. You might keep only your version, only their version, or combine the two into one cleaner result.

Sixth, delete all three marker lines. That includes the opening marker line, the middle separator line, and the closing marker line.

Seventh, review the file and confirm that no conflict markers remain. Search again for the opening marker. You should get zero results.

Eighth, commit the changes on your fix branch.

Ninth, open a pull request. The suggested title is fix: resolve conflict markers in filename. In the body, include Closes issue-number and one or two sentences explaining what you kept and why.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
I love that the instructions don't just say remove the markers. They also ask learners to explain their content decision.

[ALEX]
Yes, because randomly deleting text is not conflict resolution. Intentional selection is.

[JAMIE]
What about accessibility support in that challenge?

[ALEX]
There is a specific screen reader tip. Use your find command to jump directly to the markers. In a browser, that's typically Control F. In VS Code, learners may also use find. The key point is that the markers are plain text, so they are fully readable to screen readers.

[JAMIE]
That's reassuring. No hidden visual trick, just text.

[ALEX]
Exactly. And the done condition is also concrete: the pull request passes bot validation checks and contains no remaining conflict markers.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Once the PR is open, what evidence do learners submit?

[ALEX]
They return to their assigned challenge issue and post a completion comment. The format is straightforward: Chapter 7 completed, then a bullet noting the PR number and file, and another bullet stating the content decision they made and why.

[JAMIE]
So the issue, branch, PR, and comment all connect together.

[ALEX]
Right. That linkage is part of good contribution workflow.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
The expected outcomes for the chapter are also worth naming plainly. By the end, a learner should be able to recognize the three conflict marker lines immediately, read both sides of a conflict, make an intentional decision, remove all markers, and submit a clean issue-linked PR.

[JAMIE]
And if they get stuck?

[ALEX]
The course gives very practical guidance. If you can't find the markers, search for the opening marker string. They always appear in sets. If you're unsure which side to keep, read both versions aloud and pick the clearer one, or combine them. If you deleted too much, undo and try that section again. If a PR bot says the content is wrong, search again for all three marker patterns to make sure none remain. And it is completely appropriate to ask a facilitator to sanity-check your final content before you open the PR.

[JAMIE]
There's also a reference solution, right?

[ALEX]
Yes. If a learner finishes but still feels unsure, they can compare their work to the chapter's reference solution.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Now let's zoom out to the bigger lesson. Merge conflicts are not failures. They are a normal checkpoint in collaboration. In real open source work, they happen whenever people edit near the same lines. The skill is not to magically avoid every conflict forever. The skill is to resolve them clearly and calmly.

[JAMIE]
And the chapter's learning pattern supports that confidence.

[ALEX]
It does. Start with a safe, controlled conflict. Learn the structure. Make a deliberate decision. Submit evidence through the normal pull request workflow. Build confidence for future real-world conflicts.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
There's also a note about learning cards in this chapter.

[ALEX]
Yes, and we should include that because it's part of the learner support design. This chapter uses expandable learning cards tailored to different ways of working. Not every card appears at every step, so learners are encouraged to open the ones that match their setup.

The five card types are: visual or mouse guidance for sighted users; low vision guidance for magnification, zoom, and high contrast workflows; NVDA and JAWS guidance for Windows screen reader users; VoiceOver guidance for macOS users; and CLI guidance for terminal users.

[JAMIE]
So accessibility here is not an afterthought. It is built into the chapter structure.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before we get into prevention strategies, can we cover the local Git alternative?

[ALEX]
Definitely. The main teaching path in this chapter uses the GitHub web conflict editor, but there is a local Git option for learners who cloned the repository earlier and prefer terminal workflows.

The steps are: go into the repository folder, check out main, pull the latest main from origin, switch back to your branch, and merge main into your branch. If there is a conflict, Git reports the affected files and stops the merge.

Then open the conflicted file in your editor, maybe with VS Code. Inside the file you will see the conflict markers showing your version, the separator, and the incoming version from main.

Edit the file. Keep the version you want, or combine both. Delete all three marker lines. Save the file.

Then mark the file resolved with git add, create a commit such as Resolve merge conflict in filename, and push. Your pull request on GitHub updates automatically.

[JAMIE]
And the same checks and review still apply.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Different workspace, same collaboration rules.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Let's talk about why conflicts happen in the first place. The most common causes are pretty predictable.

Two people edit the same line.

One person deletes a file while another edits it.

Two people restructure the same section in different ways.

Or a pull request stays open for a long time and drifts farther and farther away from main.

[JAMIE]
That last one feels especially common.

[ALEX]
It is. Long-running branches tend to collect conflict risk.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Okay, so how do we prevent conflicts without becoming afraid to collaborate?

[ALEX]
Great question. The chapter emphasizes that prevention is easier than resolution, and it gives a practical list.

First, keep branches short-lived. Small, focused work merged quickly usually produces fewer conflicts than branches that linger for weeks. A useful target is roughly one to three days from branch creation to merge. If the work is larger, break it into smaller pull requests.

Second, sync with main frequently. If main keeps moving and your branch never checks in, you increase the chance of painful surprises later.

From your feature branch, fetch the latest changes and merge origin slash main into your branch. If you are comfortable with rebasing, rebasing onto origin slash main is another option, but that assumes you understand rebase and its tradeoffs.

[JAMIE]
So the idea is not just pull once at the beginning and hope for the best.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Stay current.

Third, communicate with your team. If you know you'll be editing a shared file, say so. A quick message can prevent duplicated work and awkward overlap.

Fourth, avoid mass reformatting unless it is planned. Huge whitespace-only changes, big reorganizations, or style rewrites make conflicts much more likely for everyone else.

Fifth, pull before you push. Make sure you are integrating recent remote changes instead of trying to land outdated work.

Sixth, work on separate files when possible. Sometimes work can be divided in ways that reduce overlap.

Seventh, keep pull requests small. Smaller PRs are easier to review, easier to merge, and less likely to drift.

Eighth, use draft pull requests for early visibility. Even before the work is done, a draft PR helps others see what area you are touching.

[JAMIE]
That's such a useful social signal. It says, I'm working here.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Conflict prevention is partly technical and partly communicative.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
There's also an advanced prevention concept in the chapter: fast-forward merges. Can you unpack that without going too deep into Git theory?

[ALEX]
Sure. A fast-forward merge happens when the target branch has not moved ahead independently, so Git can simply move the branch pointer forward. No merge commit is needed, and there is no competing history to combine at that moment.

[JAMIE]
So in a sense, the cleanest merge is one where there was never a divergence to reconcile.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Understanding fast-forward merges helps learners see why staying up to date and merging quickly can reduce complexity.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
I noticed a section called when conflicts are actually good. That sounds counterintuitive.

[ALEX]
It does, but it's important. Sometimes a conflict is a useful safety signal. It means Git refused to make a silent guess about overlapping edits. Instead, it asked a human to choose intentionally.

[JAMIE]
So a conflict can protect meaning.

[ALEX]
Precisely. If two people changed the same accessibility instruction, keyboard shortcut, or critical sentence in different ways, you want that pause. It gives you a chance to combine the best ideas or choose the clearer wording instead of letting one overwrite the other without review.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's move to the very practical question: how do you spot a conflict on GitHub?

[ALEX]
On a pull request, GitHub may indicate that the branch has conflicts that must be resolved before merging. In other words, the PR is not merge-ready yet. That status message is your cue to inspect the conflicting files.

[JAMIE]
And the tool card idea here is basically: resolve a merge conflict by editing the file and removing the markers.

[ALEX]
Exactly. The heart of the task is always the same. Open the conflicting file. Remove the marker lines. Keep the content you actually want.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Now let's spend real time on conflict markers, because once learners understand the markers, a lot of fear disappears.

A conflicted file contains three special marker lines.

The opening marker, made of left angle brackets, marks the start of the conflict region.

The middle line of equals signs separates the two versions.

The closing marker, made of right angle brackets, marks the end of the conflict region and often names the incoming branch.

[JAMIE]
And between those markers, one block is your version and one block is their version.

[ALEX]
Right. Usually the top block, between the opening marker and the equals line, is the current branch version. The bottom block, between the equals line and the closing marker, is the incoming version.

[JAMIE]
Could we do a plain-language example?

[ALEX]
Yes. Imagine a markdown table in a file about keyboard shortcuts. Before the conflict, there was one existing row. Then two students both edited that same row area to add different shortcut information. When Git tries to combine them, the file may end up showing both edits wrapped in conflict markers.

One resolution option is to keep the first student's row.

Another is to keep the second student's row.

A better option in many cases is to combine both additions into one clean, correctly formatted table so no information is lost.

[JAMIE]
That's the key idea: the resolution isn't always choosing sides. Sometimes it's synthesizing.

[ALEX]
Exactly. And after that decision, all the marker lines must be removed. If any marker remains, the file is still unresolved.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
How does conflict resolution work in the GitHub web editor?

[ALEX]
The chapter teaches the web editor as the primary method. The step-by-step flow is roughly this: open the pull request or conflict prompt, choose the option to resolve conflicts, move through each conflicted file, edit the content directly in the browser, remove the markers, keep the final clean text, mark the conflict resolved, and complete the commit that updates the branch.

[JAMIE]
What does it look like in the editor?

[ALEX]
Visually, GitHub may show the conflicted region clearly, but the important point for blind and low-vision learners is that the underlying content is text. Screen reader users can navigate by line, search for the marker strings, and read both versions directly. Low-vision users can increase zoom, use high contrast themes, and rely on the strong textual markers rather than color alone.

[JAMIE]
So even if the interface has visual cues, the lesson still works text-first.

[ALEX]
Exactly. That's why the learning cards matter. A visual learner might use click targets and color-coded regions. A low-vision learner might enlarge text and inspect marker visibility. NVDA, JAWS, and VoiceOver users may rely on find, line navigation, and careful reading of the plain-text markers.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
What about VS Code on day two?

[ALEX]
In VS Code, conflicts are often shown with special indicators and action choices. You may see labels for current change and incoming change, and quick actions such as accept current, accept incoming, accept both, or compare changes.

[JAMIE]
That sounds convenient, but also potentially dangerous if someone clicks too quickly.

[ALEX]
Exactly right. Those commands are helpful, but they should support your thinking, not replace it. Learners should still read both sides carefully. Sometimes accept both is correct. Sometimes it creates duplicated or awkward content. Sometimes neither version should be kept exactly as written, and you need to edit manually.

[JAMIE]
So VS Code gives you tools, but your judgment still matters.

[ALEX]
Always.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's talk directly to the learner who feels frozen when they see a conflict.

[ALEX]
Yes. If you feel stuck, first remember that asking for help is normal. Conflicts happen to experienced developers too. A teammate or facilitator can often confirm your interpretation in a minute or two.

Second, there is a nuclear option: abandon the attempt and start fresh. If your branch became messy and you are no longer confident, it may be faster to back out, recreate a clean branch from updated main, and reapply the intended change carefully.

[JAMIE]
That's important. Starting over is not defeat.

[ALEX]
Not at all. Sometimes it is the most professional choice.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Can we cover what a conflict message looks like from the Git command line?

[ALEX]
Absolutely. This is a useful reference workflow.

Step one: start the merge that causes the conflict. For example, while on your branch, merge main into it.

Step two: Git tells you there was a conflict and lists files with conflict status. You are especially looking for entries that say both modified.

Step three: open each conflicted file in your editor.

Inside the file, edit the content. Remove the opening markers, separator, and closing markers. Keep the content you want.

Step four: after editing, mark each resolved file with git add.

Step five: complete the merge with a commit. Git usually auto-fills the merge commit message for you.

Then check the result. View the pull request status. Confirm the merge state is now healthy. Check all PR checks and merge readiness. And review the diff so you understand exactly what changed.

[JAMIE]
I like that final step. Don't just trust that it worked. Inspect the result.

[ALEX]
Yes. Verification matters.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Let's do a quick summary checklist in plain language.

Know what a merge conflict is: overlapping edits Git cannot decide between.

Know why conflicts happen: same-line edits, delete-versus-edit situations, structural overlap, and long-diverged branches.

Prevent them when possible: short-lived branches, frequent sync with main, communication, smaller PRs, separate files when possible, and early visibility through draft PRs.

Recognize the three conflict markers immediately.

Read both sides before making any decision.

Keep one side, the other side, or combine both intentionally.

Delete all marker lines.

Commit, push, and verify the pull request is clean and passing checks.

[JAMIE]
And emotionally, read a conflict without fear.

[ALEX]
Exactly. That is one of the chapter's quiet goals. A conflict message should become something you can inspect, decode, and solve, not something that makes you panic.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before we close, can you say a word about sources and trust?

[ALEX]
Yes. This lesson is grounded in the official GitHub documentation, the Git documentation, GitHub flow guidance, and pull request guidance. That matters because merge conflict workflows can vary a little across tools, but the underlying principles remain stable.

[JAMIE]
So if a learner remembers only one sentence?

[ALEX]
A merge conflict is just Git asking for a human decision about overlapping changes.

[JAMIE]
And if they remember two?

[ALEX]
The second is this: read both sides, keep what belongs, remove the markers, and verify the result.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
You've got this. Conflicts are part of real collaboration, including accessible and open source workflows. The more calmly you practice them, the more confident you become.

[JAMIE]
And that confidence carries across GitHub, VS Code, and the terminal.

[ALEX]
Exactly. See you next time.

sourceFiles.content:
# Merge Conflicts
>
> **Listen to Episode 7:** [Merge Conflicts Are Not Scary](https://lp.csedesigns.com/ggg/PODCASTS.html) - a conversational audio overview of this chapter. Listen before reading to preview the concepts, or after to reinforce what you learned.

> **Related appendices:** [Appendix E: Advanced Git](appendix-e-advanced-git.md) | [Appendix G: VS Code Reference](appendix-g-vscode-reference.md)
> **Authoritative sources:** [GitHub Docs: Resolving merge conflicts](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/collaborating-with-pull-requests/addressing-merge-conflicts/resolving-a-merge-conflict-on-github) | [Git SCM: Basic Merge Conflicts](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Branching-Basic-Branching-and-Merging#_basic_merge_conflicts)

## Understanding, Preventing, and Resolving Conflicts

> Merge conflicts sound intimidating but are a normal, manageable part of collaborative development. This guide explains what conflicts are, how to read conflict markers, and how to resolve them - step by step.

## Workshop Recommendation (Chapter 7)

Chapter 7 uses **one controlled practice challenge** so students can learn conflict resolution without high-pressure scenarios.

- **Challenge count:** 1
- **Time:** under 10 minutes
- **Evidence:** issue-linked PR and completion comment
- **Pattern:** observe, resolve, verify

### Chapter 7 Challenge Set

1. **Resolve conflict markers** - identify and clean up conflict markers in a practice file, then open a linked PR.

> **Branch guidance for Chapter 7:** Use a short-lived feature branch: `fix/yourname-issueXX` (for example, `fix/maria-issue48`). The same pattern you used in Chapter 6.

### Challenge 7.1 Step-by-Step: Resolve Conflict Markers

**Goal:** Identify the three types of conflict markers in a practice file, decide which content to keep, remove the markers, and submit a clean PR.

> **Agentic strategy:** Sometimes an AI agent will confidently generate code that conflicts with human-written code. Resolving merge conflicts is not just a hurdle for human teamwork; it is exactly how you supervise, correct, and collaborate safely with an AI.

**Where you are working:** your Learning Room repository on GitHub.com (web editor) or in VS Code if you cloned locally.

**Before you start:** Open your **assigned Chapter 7 challenge issue** (the one titled "Chapter 7.1: Resolve Conflict Markers (@yourname)"). The issue description tells you which practice file contains the conflict markers.

Practice sample: [`learning-room/docs/samples/chapter-6-conflict-practice-sample.md`](../learning-room/docs/samples/chapter-6-conflict-practice-sample.md)

1. Open the practice file specified in your challenge issue.
2. Search the file for `<<<<<<<`. This is the **start marker** - it shows where the conflict begins.
3. Read the content between `<<<<<<<` and `=======`. This is **your version** (the current branch).
4. Read the content between `=======` and `>>>>>>>`. This is **their version** (the incoming branch).
5. Decide which content to keep:
   - Keep only your version, or
   - Keep only their version, or
   - Combine both versions into one clean paragraph.
6. Delete all three marker lines:
   - The `<<<<<<< HEAD` line (or similar)
   - The `=======` separator line
   - The `>>>>>>> branch-name` line
7. Review the file to confirm no marker lines remain. Search for `<<<<<<<` again - there should be zero results.
8. Commit your changes on a branch named `fix/yourname-issueXX`.
9. Open a pull request with:
   - Title: `fix: resolve conflict markers in [filename]`
   - Body: Include `Closes #XX` (your challenge issue number) and a 1-2 sentence description of which content you kept and why.

**Screen reader tip:** Use your screen reader's find command (`Ctrl+F` in browser, `Ctrl+H` in VS Code) to jump directly to `<<<<<<<`. The markers are plain text, so they are fully readable.

**You are done when:** Your PR passes bot validation checks and contains no remaining conflict markers.

### Completing Chapter 7: Submit Your Evidence

When your PR is open and passing checks, post a comment on your assigned Chapter 7 challenge issue:

```text
Chapter 7 completed:
- Challenge 7.1: Opened PR #[number] resolving conflict markers in [filename]
- Content decision: kept [your version / their version / combined both] because [reason]
```

### Expected Outcomes

- Student can identify the three conflict marker lines (`<<<<<<<`, `=======`, `>>>>>>>`) immediately.
- Student can read both sides of a conflict and make an intentional content decision.
- Student can remove all markers and submit a clean, issue-linked PR.

### If You Get Stuck

1. Can't find the markers? Use `Ctrl+F` and search for `<<<<<<<` - they are always in sets of three.
2. Not sure which side to keep? Read both versions aloud. Pick the one that is clearer, or combine them.
3. Accidentally deleted too much? Undo with `Ctrl+Z` and start the section over.
4. PR bot says content is wrong? Double-check that zero marker lines remain - search for `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, and `>>>>>>>`.
5. Ask facilitator to sanity-check your final content before opening the PR.
6. Finished but not sure you did it right? Compare your work against the [Challenge 7 reference solution](solutions/solution-07-merge-conflict.md).

### Learning Moment

Merge conflicts are not failures. They are a normal collaboration checkpoint and a chance to make an intentional content decision. In real open source projects, conflicts happen whenever two people edit near the same lines. The skill is not avoiding them - it is resolving them calmly and clearly.

### Learning Pattern Used in This Chapter

1. Start with a controlled, safe conflict (practice file with known markers).
2. Learn to read the conflict structure (your version vs. their version).
3. Make a deliberate content decision (not just deleting randomly).
4. Submit clean evidence through the PR workflow.
5. Build confidence for real conflicts in future contributions.

### About Learning Cards in This Chapter

This chapter provides learning cards: expandable blocks that offer perspective-specific guidance for different ways of working. Not every card appears at every step. Open the ones that match how you work.

The following table describes the five learning card types used in this chapter.

| Card | Who it helps | What it covers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Visual / mouse | Sighted users navigating with a mouse or trackpad | Click targets, visual cues, color-coded conflict regions |
| Low vision | Users with magnification, zoom, or high-contrast themes | Zoom-friendly navigation, high contrast marker visibility, enlargement tips |
| NVDA / JAWS (Windows) | Screen reader users on Windows | Keystroke sequences, Focus and Browse mode, verbosity tips |
| VoiceOver (macOS) | Screen reader users on macOS | VO key sequences, rotor navigation, interaction model |
| CLI (git / gh) | Terminal users on any platform | Git and GitHub CLI commands for conflict detection and resolution |

## Local Git Alternative: Resolving Conflicts from Your Terminal

<details>
<summary>If you cloned the learning-room in Block 0 and prefer resolving conflicts locally</summary>

The GitHub web conflict editor works well and is the primary method taught in this chapter. If you cloned the Learning Room in Block 0 and prefer working in your terminal, here is how to resolve conflicts locally. This is the same workflow covered in depth in [Chapter 11: Git and Source Control](14-git-in-practice.md).

**Step 1 - Sync main and merge into your branch:**

```bash
cd ~/Documents/learning-room
git checkout main
git pull origin main
git checkout your-branch-name
git merge main
```

If there is a conflict, Git will report which files are affected and stop the merge.

**Step 2 - Open the conflicted file:**

```bash
code docs/welcome.md   # or your preferred editor
```

Look for the conflict markers:

```text
<<<<<<< HEAD
Your version of the content
=======
The incoming version from main
>>>>>>> main
```

**Step 3 - Resolve by editing:**

- Keep the version you want (or combine both)
- Delete all three marker lines (`<<<<<<<`, `=======`, `>>>>>>>`)
- Save the file

**Step 4 - Mark resolved, commit, and push:**

```bash
git add docs/welcome.md
git commit -m "Resolve merge conflict in welcome.md"
git push
```

Your PR on GitHub updates automatically with the resolved content. The same bot checks and human review process apply.

</details>

## What Is a Merge Conflict?

A merge conflict occurs when two people have both changed the **same part of the same file** in **different ways**, and Git cannot automatically decide which version is correct.

Git can merge changes automatically when they touch different parts of a file. Conflicts only happen when two changes overlap - for example:

- Person A changed line 12 to say "Submit form"
- Person B changed line 12 to say "Send message"
- Git asks: which one do you want to keep?

## Why Conflicts Happen

The most common causes:

| Cause | Example |
| -------  | ---------  |
| Two people edited the same line | You both fixed the same typo differently |
| One person deleted a file but another edited it | You removed an old function; they fixed a bug in it |
| Two people restructured the same section | You reorganized a list; they added items to it |
| A long-running PR diverged from main | Your branch is weeks old and main has changed significantly |

## How to Prevent Conflicts (Prevention is Easier Than Resolution)

Avoiding conflicts in the first place saves time and reduces stress. Here are the most effective strategies:

### 1. **Keep your branches short-lived**

Work in small, focused chunks. A branch that lives for 3 days has far fewer conflicts than one that lives for 3 weeks.

- Target: 1-3 days from branch to merge
- If a feature takes longer, break it into smaller PRs

### 2. **Sync with main frequently**

The longer your branch diverges from main, the more likely conflicts become.

**Best practice:** Sync daily if main is active:

```bash
# From your feature branch
git fetch origin
git merge origin/main
# Or: git rebase origin/main (if comfortable with rebasing)
```

**GitHub web method:** Use the "Update branch" button on your PR if it appears.

### 3. **Communicate with your team**

Let others know what files you're working on. Use issue comments:

> "Heads up: I'm working on the `[TODO]` sections in `docs/welcome.md` for Challenge 3. If you're also editing welcome.md, let's coordinate so we don't conflict."

In the Learning Room, this is especially important because multiple students may claim challenges that touch the same file. Challenges 1 and 3 both modify `docs/welcome.md` - if two students work on both simultaneously without coordinating, a merge conflict will occur.

### 4. **Avoid mass reformatting**

Running a formatter on an entire file creates conflicts with anyone else editing that file. If you must:

- Do it in a **separate PR** before functional changes
- Announce it to the team
- Merge it quickly so everyone can sync

### 5. **Pull before you push**

Always fetch and merge (or pull) before pushing your changes:

```bash
git pull origin main  # Sync your local main
git checkout your-branch
git merge main        # Merge main into your branch
git push              # Now push
```

This catches conflicts locally where they're easier to resolve.

### 6. **Work on separate files when possible**

If multiple people are working simultaneously, divide tasks by files or modules rather than everyone touching the same code.

### 7. **Keep PRs small**

A 50-file PR will almost certainly conflict with something. A 5-file PR merges quickly and cleanly.

The most effective contributors make many small PRs rather than one giant one.

### 8. **Use Draft PRs for early visibility**

Open your PR as a draft while still working. Others can see what you're changing and avoid overlapping work. Convert to "Ready for review" when done.

## Advanced Prevention: Understanding Fast-Forward Merges

When your branch is perfectly up to date with main and adds new commits on top, GitHub can do a "fast-forward" merge - main simply moves forward to your latest commit. No merge commit needed. No possibility of conflicts.

**How to achieve this:** Rebase your branch on main right before merging:

```bash
git checkout your-branch
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main
git push --force-with-lease  # See warning below about force pushing
```

**Warning:** Force pushing rewrites history. Only do this on branches you alone control (not shared branches). Never force push to `main`.

For more on force pushing and rebasing, see the [Glossary](appendix-a-glossary.md#force-push).

## When Conflicts Are Actually Good

Conflicts indicate that multiple people are actively improving the project. In a healthy, collaborative environment, occasional conflicts are normal and manageable.

If you never have conflicts, it might mean:

- You're the only contributor (less review, less learning)
- PRs are moving too slowly (stagnation)
- People are avoiding working on important files (technical debt)

**The goal isn't zero conflicts.** The goal is catching them early, resolving them cleanly, and learning patterns that reduce future conflicts.

## Conflict Markers - What They Mean

When conflict markers appear in a file, your editor is showing you both versions of the conflicted content so you can choose. The format is always:

```text
<<<<<<< HEAD
The content that is on YOUR current branch
=======
The content coming from the OTHER branch (or main)
>>>>>>> branch-name-or-commit-hash
```

### Breakdown

- `<<<<<<< HEAD` - the start of YOUR version (HEAD = "the branch you are currently on")
- `=======` - the dividing line between the two versions
- `>>>>>>> branch-name` - the end of the INCOMING version (from the branch being merged in)

### Example in a real file

#### Original file (`docs/keyboard-shortcuts.md`) before conflict

```markdown
| Insert+Space | Toggle between Browse Mode and Focus Mode |
```

#### After two students both added a shortcut to the same table row

```
<<<<<<< HEAD
  Insert+Space -- Toggle between Browse Mode and Focus Mode
  Insert+F5 -- List elements by type
=======
  Insert+Space -- Toggle between Browse Mode and Focus Mode
  Insert+F7 -- Elements list (links, headings, form fields)
>>>>>>> add-nvda-shortcut
```

#### Resolution options

1. Keep your version: add only `Insert+F5`
2. Keep their version: add only `Insert+F7`
3. Keep both rows: add both shortcuts to the table (often the right answer when two students added different valid shortcuts)

### Learning Cards: Conflict Markers

<details>
<summary>Screen reader users</summary>

- Conflict markers are three lines: `<<<<<<< HEAD`, `=======`, and `>>>>>>> branch-name`; your screen reader may spell out each `<`, `=`, and `>` character individually
- Everything between `<<<<<<< HEAD` and `=======` is YOUR version; everything between `=======` and `>>>>>>>` is the INCOMING version
- After resolving, search the file for `<<<<` using `Ctrl+F` to verify no markers remain; any leftover markers will break the file

</details>

<details>
<summary>Low vision users</summary>

- In GitHub's conflict editor, each version is highlighted with a different background color (typically green for yours, blue for incoming); high-contrast themes use bolder system colors
- The three marker lines (`<<<`, `===`, `>>>`) span the full width of the editor; look for rows that contain only repeated symbols
- After resolving, zoom in on the edited area and confirm the marker lines are completely deleted, not just partially removed

</details>

<details>
<summary>Sighted users</summary>

- Conflict markers appear as three distinctive lines of repeated symbols: `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, and `>>>>>>>`; they visually bracket the two conflicting versions
- The `HEAD` label after `<<<<<<<` means "your current branch"; the branch name after `>>>>>>>` identifies where the incoming change came from
- After editing, delete all three marker lines plus the version you do not want; the remaining content should read naturally as valid code or Markdown

</details>

## When You Feel Stuck

### Ask for help - it's normal

If you are unsure which version to keep:

1. Leave a comment on the PR: "I have a merge conflict in `filename.js` and I'm not sure which version to keep - could someone help me understand the intent of these two changes?"
2. Tag the PR author or a maintainer with `@username`

### Abandon and start fresh (nuclear option)

If a conflict is severe (the branch diverged a lot from main):

1. Close the PR without merging
2. Start a new branch from the latest `main`
3. Apply only your intended changes to the new branch
4. Open a new PR

This is legitimate - not a failure.

## Reading a Conflict Message from Git (Command Line Reference)

If you work locally, `git merge` or `git pull` will say:

```text
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in src/index.html
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.
```

And `git status` will show:

```text
both modified: src/index.html
```

These are normal outputs. The conflict markers are inserted into the file by Git - open the file and follow the steps above.

<details>
<summary>Git CLI alternative - resolving conflicts in the terminal</summary>

Resolve merge conflicts entirely from the command line:

```bash
# 1. Start the merge that causes the conflict
git merge main

# 2. See which files have conflicts
git status
# Look for "both modified:" entries

# 3. Open each conflicted file in your editor
# Edit the file: remove <<<<<<, =======, >>>>>> markers
# Keep the content you want

# 4. After editing, mark the file as resolved
git add src/index.html

# 5. Complete the merge
git commit
# Git auto-fills the merge commit message

# Check the result
git log --oneline -3
```

</details>

<details>
<summary>GitHub CLI (gh) alternative - checking PR conflict status</summary>

Check whether a PR has conflicts without opening a browser:

```bash
# View PR status (shows merge state)
gh pr view 42

# Check all PR checks and merge readiness
gh pr checks 42

# View the diff to understand what changed
gh pr diff 42
```

If conflicts exist, the `gh pr view` output shows "This branch has conflicts that must be resolved." Resolve locally using `git merge` (above) then push, or use the web editor.

</details>

## Summary Checklist

```text
Before you start:
  □ My PR is small and focused (fewer conflicts = easier life)
  □ I checked that others aren't editing the same files

When you see a conflict:
  □ Don't panic - conflicts are normal
  □ Read both versions (between <<< and ===, and between === and >>>)
  □ Decide: keep one, keep both, or combine intelligently
  □ Remove ALL three conflict marker lines (<<<, ===, >>>)
  □ Verify the final file makes sense
  □ Mark as resolved → Commit merge

After resolving:
  □ Re-check that the PR description and issue link are still accurate
  □ Comment on the PR: "Resolved merge conflict - kept both the aria-label and type attribute"
  □ Request re-review if reviewers already approved before the conflict was introduced
```

## Try It: Read a Conflict (Without Fear)

**Time:** 2 minutes | **What you need:** Any text editor or just read below

Read this merge conflict aloud. The goal is not to resolve it - just to understand what you're hearing:

```text
The button should have an
<<<<<<< HEAD
aria-label="Submit form"
=======
aria-label="Send your response"
>>>>>>> feature-branch
attribute for screen readers.
```

Answer these three questions:

1. **What does your branch say?** (The text between `<<<<<<< HEAD` and `=======`)
2. **What does the other branch say?** (The text between `=======` and `>>>>>>>`)
3. **Which version would you keep, and why?**

**You're done.** You just read a merge conflict. That's the entire skill - everything else is just choosing which lines to keep and deleting the three marker lines.

> **What success feels like:** Conflicts aren't mysterious anymore. They're just two versions side by side with markers telling you which is which. You already know how to pick the right one.

> ### Day 2 Amplifier - Copilot Chat & Conflict Prevention
>
> **Resolve at least one conflict completely by hand before using any AI assistance.** You must be able to read `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, and `>>>>>>>` markers and understand what each version represents. An AI-suggested resolution you cannot independently verify is a liability - you are accepting a change you do not understand into a codebase other people depend on.
>
> Once you have mastered manual conflict resolution:
>
> - **In VS Code** - Copilot Chat (`Ctrl+Alt+I`, or **Chat: Open Chat** from the Command Palette if your keymap differs) can explain a conflict in plain language - *"Person A renamed the button to 'Submit Form'; Person B renamed it to 'Send Message'. Which intent should take priority?"* - but you decide what survives
> - **In your repo** - Accessibility Agents' `@pr-review` can identify high-risk overlapping changes before a conflict occurs, flagging when two contributors are editing the same file area and giving you time to coordinate before it escalates
> - **In the cloud** - GitHub Agentic Workflows can detect stale PRs diverging from `main` and automatically notify contributors with a suggested rebase checklist - preventing the conflict before it is ever introduced
>
> *Understanding conflict markers is not a stepping stone to letting AI handle conflicts. It is the skill that tells you when AI got it wrong.*

currentFacts: The Accessibility Agents collection grows over time. Refer to it as a living catalog rather than asserting a fixed count of agents.
Challenge 15 (Discover Accessibility Agents) is browse-first. Learners are not required to fork the accessibility-agents repository to complete it.
Completing Challenge 15 unlocks Challenge 16 (Capstone Project) plus Bonus Challenges A through E. The bonus challenges are a structured unlock path, not "things to do if you finish early".

Challenge 16 is titled "Capstone Project". It accepts contributions to Accessibility Agents, GLOW, or any other meaningful repository. Review-ready drafts and contribution plans are valid evidence of completion.
The Learning Room repository is where Day 1 contributions happen (issue, branch, commit, pull request, merge). It is provisioned per learner.
Hosts are Alex (warm expert) and Jamie (curious co-host who asks the questions learners hesitate to ask). They are colleagues, not teacher and student.
voiceRules.voiceExemplar:
[ALEX]
Welcome back. Today we're working with one of those GitHub features that quietly makes open source collaboration much easier: issue templates.

[JAMIE]
And this is a great one for people who have ever opened a blank issue form and thought, what exactly am I supposed to put here?

[ALEX]
Exactly. An issue template turns that blank box into a guided experience. Instead of guessing what maintainers need, contributors get prompts, structure, and clear required fields. That reduces back-and-forth, improves quality, and helps teams act on issues faster.

[JAMIE]
So this is not just about formatting. It's about making contributions clearer and more usable.

[ALEX]
Yes, and especially in accessibility work. If someone is reporting an accessibility barrier, a vague report can be hard to reproduce. A thoughtful template can ask where the problem occurred, what assistive technology was involved, what the expected behavior was, and how severe the barrier is.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before we get into the design challenge, what should learners already have in place?

[ALEX]
A few practical things. First, you should already know how to work with GitHub issues at a basic level. Second, you need a repository where you can create or edit files, usually your fork or your own repo. Third, it really helps to use an editor with YAML syntax highlighting, such as VS Code.

[JAMIE]
And some things are recommended but not strictly required, right?

[ALEX]
Right. Familiarity with GitHub Copilot can help if you want to generate variations, but it's optional. Basic terminal comfort is useful, though you can also use the GitHub web editor or github.dev. And if you already filled out the workshop registration template earlier in this course, that template becomes a learning example now.

[JAMIE]
I like that. You've already used a professional issue template, so now you reverse-engineer it.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Also, there's an administrative note here: this chapter is meant to prepare you for a later workflow using a template-building agent. The advice is to complete the manual template chapter first, then use the automation later.

[JAMIE]
And time-wise?

[ALEX]
Plan roughly two to two and a half hours if you do the exercises and some YAML troubleshooting.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
The learning pattern for this challenge is analyze, remix, create, and test.

[JAMIE]
That feels approachable. First understand an existing template, then adapt one, then optionally build another version from scratch, then verify it works.

[ALEX]
That's the idea. The workshop recommendation frames Challenge 14 as design-focused rather than automation-focused. You're producing evidence of understanding, often as an issue comment or a pull request, rather than trying to satisfy a complicated code runtime.

[JAMIE]
Though there is still one small autograded requirement in the challenge template itself.

[ALEX]
Yes. For the assigned challenge issue, the autograder checks that a YAML file exists in the repository
